articles.title: In 2019, a Maryland family moved a 255-year-old mansion 50 miles by barge; the 4,000-square-foot house travelled across Chesapeake Bay so they could give the historic building a new waterfront home
articles.summary: A 255-year-old Georgian mansion made an extraordinary 50-mile journey across the Chesapeake Bay after a Maryland family decided to move the entire 400-ton
articles.body: A 255-year-old Georgian mansion made an extraordinary 50-mile journey across the Chesapeake Bay after a Maryland family decided to move the entire 400-ton structure by barge. The move was meant to save the historic house from possible demolition and new development. According to reporting by Inside Edition, homeowner Christian Neeley spent nearly $1 million to move the historic 4,000-square-foot brick home, known as Galloway House, from Easton, Maryland, to a new waterfront property in Queenstown. The house was built between 1760 and 1764 and was moved in 2019. The unusual move required months of planning, special equipment and careful timing. The house first traveled by road before being loaded onto a barge for the two-day trip across the Chesapeake Bay.The history behind Galloway HouseGalloway House was built between 1760 and 1764 near Easton, Maryland. It was built for newlyweds William Nicols and Henrietta Maria Chamberlaine Nicols on their 600-acre plantation in Talbot County. The house is an example of Georgian architecture from the period before the American Revolution. Over the years, the house survived more than two centuries of American history. It was later left empty, and its owners said it faced neglect and the spread of suburban development. Christian Neeley and his family bought the house and planned to move it to a new home along the Wye River in Queenstown. The goal was to preserve the historic building instead of allowing it to be lost to development. Moving such a large brick house created major challenges. According to Chesapeake Bay Magazine, the house first had to travel about six miles by road to Easton Point before it could be loaded onto a barge. The land route required road closures and careful planning because of the house's size. Water transport then became the main part of the journey. The barge carried the house about 50 miles through the Chesapeake Bay to Queenstown.Preparing a 400-ton house for open waterBefore the house could be moved, crews had to support the structure and prepare it for the journey. The house was lifted and placed on a large flatbed truck for the first part of the move. Expert House Movers handled the road portion of the project. The company moved the house in four stages over four nights, beginning September 9, 2019. The slow-moving truck traveled through local roads and across Route 50 and Route 322. The house eventually reached Easton Point, where workers prepared to move it onto a large barge. The loading process faced a problem when the barge developed ballast issues and began to tip. A larger boat was needed to help with the operation. Workers built temporary ramps from flat pieces of wood and lumber so the house could move from land onto the barge. The loading process took about eight hours and required careful maneuvering.Navigating the Chesapeake BayThe water journey began after tugboats pulled the barge carrying Galloway House into the Chesapeake Bay. According to Chesapeake Bay Magazine, the barge traveled down the Tred Avon River before heading around Tilghman Island and through Eastern Bay toward the Wye River. The full water route was about 50 miles. The sight of a 400-ton, two-story brick mansion traveling on a barge attracted attention from people around Maryland. Local residents and boaters watched the unusual trip from shore and from the water. The crew also had to watch for navigation hazards, including shallow areas and sandbars. A TowBoat U.S. vessel stood by to provide local knowledge to the tugboat captain during the journey. The house left Easton Point on September 25, 2019. It then continued toward its new location in Queenstown.Offloading and permanent restorationAfter reaching the new waterfront property in Queenstown, the crew faced another difficult task, getting the 400-ton house off the barge and onto land. The house was moved from the barge onto its new property, where it could be placed on a new foundation. The Neeley family planned to restore the historic structure and make it a permanent family home. According to reporting about the move, the house was intended to be carefully restored while preserving its historic character. The Neeley family also planned additions to the building for the new property. The Maryland House and Garden Pilgrimage later reported that the Neeley family restored the original double-pile portion of the house and built two new wings to replace an 1840s kitchen addition that could not be saved. The house remains at its new site along the Wye River. By combining historic preservation with specialized moving and marine equipment, the project gave Galloway House a new home while allowing the 1760s structure to survive for future generations.You use AI every day. articles.title: From Edinburgh to Easter Island: How my stolen Ian Wright Celtic top went round the world
articles.summary: Kevin Hill's much-loved Celtic top was lost years ago but that was just the start of an international mystery.
articles.body:
It was a prank that lasted for a quarter of a century. Simple yet bewildering for its unsuspecting victim.

It began in 2001 when Kevin Hill went searching for his favourite football top.

As a kid in Aberdeen, he'd grown up as a Celtic fan - something he says that required a thick skin.

His father took him to games in Glasgow and every season, from age five, his parents bought him the latest strip.

Now 47 and living in Dunfermline, Fife, Kevin says his prized possession was one that brought together his two sporting loves.

"As much as I'm a Celtic fan my first footballing hero was Ian Wright," he says.

"I remember him playing for Arsenal and had posters of him all over my wall.

"When I started hearing the rumour that he might be coming to Celtic, it was like my dreams were coming true."

The Arsenal legend was in the sunset of his career when he signed for Celtic in 1999.

It was a fleeting spell at Parkhead that yielded three goals for the former England striker in just eight appearances.

But such was Kevin's affection that long after it was over, the green-and-white hooped jersey remained his go-to match day uniform.

It was particularly distinctive as it featured his hero's name, but not the number 17.

Kevin explained: "The reason it doesn't have a number on the back was because he hadn't actually signed yet and so we didn't know his number when I got it."

So when the strip went missing he was gutted.

Having recently moved to Edinburgh, he assumed that someone had helped themselves during a fairly raucous flat-warming party.

While he had suspicions, he could never identify the culprit.

Over time, however, his anger faded and he'd largely forgotten about it when, years later, an email arrived in his inbox from an account he didn't recognise.

It began: "Hi Kevin, remember me? Yes that's right, it's your Ian Wright Celtic strip."

The message continued: "I hope you aren't mad with me but I decided to embark on a journey of discovery."

When Kevin opened the attached photograph it featured a woman he didn't know on the London Eye holding up what appeared to be his Celtic top to the camera.

"Running through my mind was, who has done this?

"I mean bravo, it's a really good prank.

"But little did I know there were a lot more emails to follow."

A few weeks later another message arrived.

Once again it contained a photo of a complete stranger wearing Kev's prized possession – this time in Barcelona.

"The next one was Turkey, then Italy and then it went all the way to South America," Kevin recalls.

"Christ the Redeemer was one of my favourite ones.

"It made it all the way [to Brazil] and then down to Venezuela and Puerto Rico and then back up to the USA."

As 2008 gave way to 2009 the messages kept arriving until eventually the email trail went cold. It left Kevin poring over clues for who might be responsible.

"What confused me was how did they keep this going?"

"It wasn't one of my friends globetrotting, from what I could deduce they were handing [the strip] on to someone else and giving them the email address because it was always a different person in the picture.

For another decade the mystery occupied a corner of Kevin's mind.

When he met someone new he'd tell them about the adventures of "Wrighty'". That included his fiancé Cheryl.

What Kevin didn't know that their marriage would become the key to unlocking the secret.

At the wedding reception in late August, Kevin was sitting at a table with his childhood friends from Aberdeen who all started laughing as one of them handed him a parcel.

"When I opened it, I could see it was a Celtic top but then very quickly I saw the white letters of Wright.

"I knew immediately and I just couldn't believe it."

Alongside the strip was a photobook entitled "Wrighty on Tour: 25 years of adventures around the globe"

"It was the best present I could have ever been given."

"And the fact that they kept it going that long just shows how good a friendship group I've got."

Friends since their schooldays, Kris Robertson vividly remembers Kevin's fondness for his Ian Wright Celtic strip.

"He used to wear it all the time. I just remember he was very proud of it. It was his prize possession."

That affection made it the ideal source of payback after Kevin hijacked Kris's emails with the aim of embarrassing him at work.

"It was revenge," says the 48-year-old, smiling.

Revenge that took unlikely inspiration from French cinema.

Part of the plot in the 2001 movie Amelie involves the main character stealing her dad's garden gnome and sending it around the world.

"It was postcards with pictures of all these exotic locations and I thought that's perfect, I've got to do that with his strip."

The first stage of the plan involved asking another one of their other school friends to steal the strip at Kevin's flat-warming party.

Mission accomplished, the next stage of the plan required a fake email address and finding random accomplices while on his travels.

"It had to be people he wouldn't recognise, so I was just asking whoever happened to be standing there could you just hold this strip up and I'll take a photograph. That was the game really."

"I think Benicassim music festival was the first place I took it, but if I'd sent him a photo from there he would have sussed me straight away because he knew I was there.

"So I had to make sure there was quite a long delay between going places and then sending the emails."

As the strip racked up the air miles Kris kept drip-feeding the emails to his unsuspecting friend

"At one point I did get an email back [from Kevin] saying I think I've worked out who it is.

"I knew he hadn't and of course I never heard from him again. He was obviously trying to flush me out."

A great prank, however, requires a big reveal. Which, after years of deception, was something Kris agonised over.

"When he announced he was getting married, I thought this is the perfect opportunity."

When the moment arrived Kris says the confused look on Kevin's face was worth it:

"It was really good. I knew he'd appreciate the gag and finally finding out but it was actually a bit of a relief as well. I couldn't keep this going forever."

Kris's mum and dad were among those who helped him build up a bank of photos from around the UK and Europe.

Then in 2008 he took the strip with him to South America where the prank took on a life of its own.

"I met people in Peru and I gave them the strip because they were going off travelling around the world.

"They took it away with them and went to Easter Island with the big stone heads.

They went to Christ the Redeemer in Rio. They got some brilliant photos."

There is, however, a twist – a confession Kris hasn't been brave enough to make until now.

Sometime around 2013 the steady stream of photos he'd been receiving from around the world suddenly stopped.

When he contacted the last person he knew had the strip, they sheepishly confessed to losing it.

"I suppose that's the risk of sending it off around the world with complete strangers."

Kris was determined the prank he'd invested so much time and energy into wouldn't just fizzle out.

So he spent hours scouring the internet for a replacement strip and identical lettering which, in the end, he had to iron on by hand.

"I should apologise yes it was very careless of me to lose [but] a lot of love went back into the replacement."

Which raises the intriguing prospect that more than a quarter of a century on, the original "Wrighty" is out there somewhere, searching for a way home.

This epic tale of love, loss, revenge and reconciliation might still have room for another chapter.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: The CBI on Thursday filed its second chargesheet in the Rs 7,429-crore Reliance Home Finance Ltd (RHFL) alleged loan diversion case, naming 11 accused, including three senior executives of the Reliance ADA Group and seven corporate entities.The chargesheet alleges criminal conspiracy and cheating that led to massive wrongful losses for a consortium of public sector banks and financial institutions.Among the individuals charged are RHFL director and chief financial officer Amit Bapna, Reliance Capital Group MD and vice chairperson Amitabh Jhunjhunwala, Reliance Power CFO Suresh Nagarajan, and RHFL's statutory auditor Vijay Napawaliya.The seven companies named as accused include Reliance Infrastructure, Reliance Power, Reliance Big Entertainment, Reliance Broadcast Network, Reliance Business Broadcast News Holdings, Reliance MediaWorks Financial Services, and Kunjbihari Developers.According to the probe agency, RHFL borrowed funds from lending institutions and allegedly siphoned off Rs 7,429 crore through a web of intermediary and conduit entities.These funds were ultimately diverted to various Reliance ADA Group companies in direct violation of lending terms, causing substantial financial harm to the banks while wrongfully enriching the accused individuals and related companies.The investigation stems from complaints initially filed by the Union Bank of India and other public sector bank consortium members. This latest filing brings the total number of accused charged in the specific RHFL case to 15, following an initial chargesheet filed against four individuals on July 9. The CBI noted that further investigations are ongoing to determine the roles of other potential suspects.The RHFL probe is part of a broader, Supreme Court-monitored investigation into the Reliance ADA Group.The CBI's Banking Securities Fraud Branch in Delhi has registered nine FIRs against group companies, including RCom, RCFL, RTL and Reliance Capital, based on complaints from public sector banks, LIC and the EPFO.Thursday's filing marks the seventh chargesheet submitted across these interconnected cases, which have resulted in seven arrests so far, the CBI said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Bets em Ribeirão Preto: mulheres e idosos lideram endividamento | G1
articles.standfirst: Análise do Acordo Certo ouviu 237 endividados em 21 cidades. Cassino online, como o 'tigrinho', é o preferido, e quase metade dos que jogam sente ter sido enganada.
articles.summary: Pesquisa revela que mulheres e idosos são os mais afetados por dívidas de apostas online em Ribeirão Preto, com forte preferência pelo jogo do tigrinho.
articles.body:
As mulheres são maioria entre os endividados que apostam na região de Ribeirão Preto (SP), e um em cada três tem 55 anos ou mais. É o que mostra um levantamento do Acordo Certo divulgado com exclusividade ao g1 .

Segundo o estudo, as mulheres somam 50,6% desse público, participação 8 pontos percentuais maior que a média nacional. A empresa, uma plataforma online de negociação de dívidas, ouviu 237 endividados em 21 cidades, entre elas Ribeirão Preto, Franca (SP), Barretos (SP) e Sertãozinho (SP).

Para Eduardo Cavalheiro, um dos organizadores do estudo, os dois grupos chegam às apostas por caminhos diferentes. Entre as mulheres, ele aponta mães chefes de família com renda baixa. Entre os mais velhos, a renda recorrente, como a aposentadoria, e a solidão.

Jogo do Tigrinho, ou Fortune Tiger, é um jogo de caça-níquel para celulares — Foto: BBC/Reprodução/Fortune Tiger

O levantamento mostra ainda que o cassino online, como o chamado "tigrinho", é o preferido de 58,1% dos que já jogaram. Quase metade (48,1%) sente ter se sentido enganada: ficou sem o prêmio, teve a conta bloqueada ou caiu em golpe.

A dívida pesa sobre os entrevistados. Um terço (32,5%) está negativado, e 43,9% estimam que devem mais de R$ 5 mil. Cerca de 1 em cada 10 dos que já jogaram deixou de pagar uma conta ou usou empréstimo, cheque especial ou cartão para apostar nos últimos 12 meses.

Os resultados são preliminares e retratam os endividados cadastrados na plataforma que responderam ao questionário entre 31 de julho e 28 de setembro, e não toda a população da região. A metodologia completa está no fim da reportagem.

A divisão entre mulheres (50,6%) e homens (49,4%) é equilibrada, mas a presença feminina na região supera a média nacional em 8 pontos percentuais, segundo o relatório.

Para Eduardo, parte da explicação está nas "mães que estão na base da pirâmide, que estão ali ganhando entre dois e quatro salários mínimos, que muitas vezes são chefes de família, são mães solo, e elas precisam de qualquer coisa que dê uma esperança de complemento de renda".

Os dados do estudo vão na mesma direção. Entre os que apostam para aumentar a renda, pagar contas ou recuperar perdas, 56% são mulheres, e 65% têm renda familiar de até 2 salários mínimos. Nesse recorte por perfil, os percentuais somam as respostas da região e do restante do país.

Uma pesquisa nacional citada no relatório, a Mulheres & Bets, do estúdio Clarice, da Estratégia Latina e do Instituto Ideia, aponta que 72% das apostadoras têm filhos.Um em cada três tem 55 anos ou mais

Os apostadores com 55 anos ou mais somam 35,4% dos endividados ouvidos na região. Segundo Eduardo, é um público que costuma ter renda recorrente, como aposentadoria e pensão, e às vezes uma reserva construída ao longo da vida.

Ele compara o hábito ao de décadas atrás: muitos dos que jogavam bingo há 20 ou 30 anos hoje estão nas bets. E aponta um fator emocional.

"A gente está vivendo uma epidemia de solidão. Os mais velhos muitas vezes não têm tantas opções de atividade, de lazer, e acabam se entregando ao passatempo mais rápido, à dopamina que chega mais rápido", diz.

As bets costumam ser associadas ao futebol, mas a aposta em resultado esportivo quase não aparece entre os endividados da região: teve menos de 1% das respostas.

Apostas esportivas são menos frequentes na regi — Foto: Reprodução/EPTV

O que domina são jogos como "Tigrinho", "Dragão" e similares, que imitam máquinas caça-níqueis. Outros 3,2% preferem jogos específicos, como "Avião" e "Mines", e 38,7% dizem não jogar valendo dinheiro.

Para Eduardo, a aposta esportiva costuma ser só o começo.

"Quando a gente entra em qualquer site de apostas esportivas, você tem lá a opção do link para entrar nos jogos. Então, as apostas esportivas funcionam como porta de entrada para os jogos de cassino, para os tigrinhos, para os aviões", diz. "A dinâmica do cassino é a casa sempre ganha."

O apostador endividado da região, em geral, começou há pouco e aposta valores baixos. Seis em cada dez (61,3%) jogam há menos de seis meses, pouco mais da metade (54,8%) joga algumas vezes por mês, e dois em cada três (67,7%) gastam até R$ 50 por mês.

Segundo Eduardo, o valor baixo não diminui o problema.

"Sobrou um troco, sobrou 10 reais, sobrou 15 reais, a plataforma aceita qualquer valor. Então os menores valores, que muitas vezes são para complementar uma despesa de supermercado, estão indo para as apostas, e isso é muito preocupante."

Quem joga sabe do risco: para 87,1%, esporte, cassino e outros jogos são todos jogos de azar. A publicidade aparece pouco nas respostas: 12,9% disseram ter jogado motivados por propaganda ou influenciadores, e 7,4% seguem influenciadores ou grupos de palpites.

Jogo do tigrinho: a 'conta demo' usada por influenciadores para mostrar 'ganhos' — Foto: Reprodução Fantástico

O próprio relatório faz uma ressalva: os entrevistados tendem a declarar menos frequência e valores menores do que de fato apostam.

A preferência pelo cassino importa porque essa modalidade tem a maior taxa estimada de jogo problemático entre os formatos analisados por uma revisão sistemática publicada na revista científica The Lancet Public Health. Entre usuários de cassinos online e caça-níqueis virtuais, a taxa chegou a 15,8%. O índice se refere a quem usa essas plataformas, e não à população em geral.

Os 48,1% que se sentiram enganados reúnem três situações: não receber o prêmio, ter a conta bloqueada ou cair em golpe, uma ou mais vezes.

Perder dinheiro que não pode perder é a principal preocupação de 25,9%. Cair em golpe preocupa 18,5%. Um terço (33,3%), porém, diz não ter medo das consequências.

Se ganhassem dinheiro extra nas apostas, 63,6% dos endividados ouvidos usariam o valor para pagar dívidas. Outros 26,2% guardariam o dinheiro, e 10,3% quitariam contas atrasadas.

Entre os negativados, três em cada quatro colocariam o dinheiro na dívida, tanto na região (75,3%) quanto no restante do país (76,5%).

"As pessoas estão deixando muitas vezes de quitar uma dívida para poder apostar e fazer uma renda extra para cobrir o mês, para chegar no final do mês", afirma Eduardo.

Entre os que deixaram de pagar uma conta por causa do jogo, cerca de 6 em cada 10 usaram crédito para conseguir apostar. Segundo Eduardo, desde a pandemia, famílias que já viviam "na corda bamba do orçamento" se endividaram ainda mais, muitas vezes usando o único crédito que tinham, e o mais caro: o rotativo do cartão.

Dois em cada três entrevistados (67,1%) têm renda familiar de até 4 salários mínimos. A faixa mais citada é a de 2 a 4 salários (32,9%).

O levantamento compara a região de Ribeirão Preto com 430 endividados ouvidos no restante do país. Na região, 32,5% dos entrevistados estão negativados. Fora dela, são 54%.

O motivo para apostar também muda. Na região, a maioria dos que já jogaram (58%) aposta principalmente por diversão ou emoção. No restante do país, esse grupo é de 31%. Já quem aposta por necessidade representa 29% dos apostadores da região e 54% no restante do país.

Segundo a empresa, os entrevistados da região têm renda maior e estão menos negativados, o que explica boa parte das diferenças. Por isso, a comparação serve de referência, e não de ranking.

O levantamento do Acordo Certo é um estudo quantitativo, feito 100% pela internet. O questionário foi enviado por e-mail a usuários da plataforma que têm dívida cadastrada.

Na região, foram 237 entrevistas em 21 municípios, entre 31 de julho e 28 de setembro de 2026. Segundo a empresa, a margem de erro é de 6,4 pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, com nível de confiança de 95%.

As perguntas sobre hábitos de jogo, como frequência, gasto, preferência e motivação, foram respondidas só por quem já jogou. Por isso, esses percentuais têm uma base menor que o total de entrevistados, e a margem de erro nesses recortes é maior.

Os resultados são preliminares, já que o formulário segue aberto, e representam os endividados cadastrados que responderam à pesquisa, não a população da região. A empresa aponta ainda três limitações: a amostra vem de uma base de pessoas com dívida, os entrevistados tendem a declarar menos frequência e valor apostado, e a coleta foi feita só pela internet, em um período específico do ano.

A coleta terminou três dias depois da publicação da medida provisória que proíbe as apostas online no país, em 25 de setembro.

articles.summary: O Centro Integrado Sesc Senac fica localizado na rua João Batista Cordeiro, no Jardim Campomar.
articles.body:
Formação presencial inclui cursos de beleza e informática, com turmas previstas para começar em setembro — Foto: Divulgação

Quem busca uma nova profissão ou quer ampliar os conhecimentos para o mercado de trabalho encontra no Centro Integrado Sesc Senac oportunidades de qualificação em diferentes áreas. A unidade de Rio das Ostras oferece cursos presenciais de gastronomia, saúde, tecnologia e beleza, com turmas previstas para começar entre setembro e outubro de 2026.

As formações atendem desde quem deseja iniciar uma carreira até profissionais que buscam aperfeiçoar suas habilidades, com aulas práticas e conteúdos voltados à atuação profissional. A ação tem o apoio da Secretaria de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Turismo.

O Centro Integrado Sesc Senac fica localizado na rua João Batista Cordeiro, no Jardim Campomar (rua do Renascer da Terceira Idade). Mais informações sobre os cursos, inscrições, matrículas e valores podem ser consultados pelo link .

CURSOS – Na área de gastronomia, o curso “Pizzas: Segredos e Receitas que São Massa” prepara os alunos para o preparo de pizzas básicas, aplicação de técnicas específicas e procedimentos de segurança alimentar. A formação tem carga horária de 52 horas, aulas às terças-feiras, das 18h às 22h, e previsão de início em 13 de outubro de 2026, com término em 26 de janeiro de 2027.

Outra opção é o curso “Bolos e Geleias Para Ganhar uma Bolada”, que aborda técnicas de preparo, segurança alimentar, congelamento, precificação, planejamento de vendas e divulgação de produtos. Com 24 horas de duração, as aulas acontecem de quarta a sexta-feira, das 8h às 12h. A turma está prevista para o período de 13 de novembro a 4 de dezembro de 2026.

Para quem pretende ingressar na área da saúde, o curso Técnico em Enfermagem oferece formação com 1.600 horas, incluindo conhecimentos técnicos, práticas em laboratório e estágio supervisionado. As aulas são presenciais, de segunda a sexta-feira, das 18h às 22h, com início previsto para 19 de outubro de 2026 e término em 13 de julho de 2028.

A programação também inclui oportunidades para quem deseja desenvolver competências digitais. O curso “Inteligência Artificial Sem Mistério, Turbinando Sua Produtividade” ensina, na prática, o uso de ferramentas como ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, Gamma e Leonardo AI para criação de textos, imagens, apresentações e vídeos. São 16 horas de formação, com aulas aos sábados, das 9h às 13h, entre 24 de outubro e 14 de novembro de 2026.

Já o curso Informática Fundamental aborda o uso do computador, da internet e dos aplicativos do Pacote Office, em aulas práticas no laboratório de Tecnologia da Informação. A formação tem 60 horas, com um computador por aluno, e está prevista para acontecer aos sábados, das 9h às 13h, de 19 de setembro de 2026 a 23 de janeiro de 2027.

Na área de beleza, o curso “Alongamento de Cílios” prepara profissionais para técnicas como fio a fio, volume russo, híbrida e extensões de 2D a 6D. São 24 horas de aulas aos sábados, das 9h às 13h, com início em 26 de setembro e término em 31 de outubro de 2026.

O curso “Práticas do Trabalho do Cabeleireiro” é voltado a quem deseja iniciar uma carreira profissional em corte, coloração, modelagem e tratamentos dos fios. A formação tem 100 horas, com aulas às quartas-feiras, das 18h às 22h, e previsão de realização de 14 de outubro de 2026 a 28 de abril de 2027.

articles.summary: Aaron Wood, a Texas professor, allegedly sent sexually explicit photos and messages online to an undercover Florida officer he believed was a 14-year-old boy.
articles.body: Texas officials last week arrested a Dallas-area community college professor accused of sending sexually explicit photos and messages online to an individual he believed was a 14-year-old boy. Aaron Wood, 34, who taught drama for two years at North Central Texas College (NCTC), allegedly sent the messages on Snapchat to an undercover agent in Florida May 22. The Denton County Sheriff’s Office arrested Wood Friday and charged him with solicitation of a minor via computer, according to county records. The school confirmed his arrest in a statement, saying he was no longer employed as of Monday. FORMER TEXAS HIGH SCHOOL TEACHER ARRESTED AFTER PROBE INTO INAPPROPRIATE STUDENT RELATIONSHIP NCTC added the alleged offense did not involve any school staff or students. "To our knowledge, the alleged offense does not involve NCTC, its students or staff," the college said. "We can verify that he has had no contact with NCTC students, faculty or staff since his arrest on September 25, 2026." According to an arrest affidavit, Wood allegedly engaged in an online conversation on Snapchat with an undercover officer from the Orange County Sheriff’s Office in Florida, FOX 4 Dallas reported. During their interaction, Wood reportedly told the undercover officer he teaches students around the same age as the person he believed he was speaking with. FLORIDA MIDDLE SCHOOL TEACHER ADMITS TO YEARS OF 'INAPPROPRIATE' CONVERSATIONS WITH FORMER STUDENT: DEPUTIES When asked about his students, Wood allegedly told the officer he had "been into a few over the years" and that he was nervous but still interested in chatting with the undercover officer. The affidavit says Wood sent a picture of male genitals, along with other sexually explicit messages, to the officer and asked to see theirs, FOX 4 reported. Authorities tracked Wood through the IP address used during the interaction, which led them to an apartment in Denton. FORMER NORTH TEXAS POLICE OFFICER GIVEN THREE LIFE SENTENCES FOR CHILD PORNOGRAPHY, SOLICITATION OF MINOR The affidavit noted that the Orange County Sheriff’s Office had probable cause to charge Wood with transmission of harmful material to minors and unlawful use of a two-way communication device, FOX 4 reported. articles.body: Flydubai Flight 1073 was in the air when a wounded captain battled his copilot as the aircraft went into a dive, leaving passengers to rush to the cockpit and help regain control of the plane before it landed safely.Video footage showed passengers running towards the cockpit to rescue the Flydubai flight after the copilot attempted to hijack the aircraft.A dentist and other passengers wrestled with the violent copilot as the aircraft plunged towards the desert, while a plumber took control of the plane. Despite being stabbed, the captain managed to open the cockpit door, helping save around 180 people aboard the Israel-bound flight.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warmly embraced plumber Yaniv Hayoun shortly after the passengers arrived in Tel Aviv late on Wednesday. He later praised Hayoun’s actions, calling him “a hero who has saved many lives.” Hayoun was among several Israelis recommended for the Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism, while Indian Capt. Smit Machchhar was hailed as “a Hero” by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.Dr Shota Musaev, a dentist travelling on the flight, was among the passengers who rushed towards the cockpit. He told CNN that he found the attacker on top of Machchhar, stabbing him.Musaev said the captain was covered in cuts, particularly on his head and hands, and had lost a large amount of blood. Fearing that Machchhar might die before help arrived, Musaev helped restrain the attacker, using headphone cords and plastic zip ties to tie him up.The identity of the flight’s co-pilot has not been publicly disclosed. An Omani official told CBS News that the assailant was born in Oman and holds Omani citizenship, although Muscat has not formally confirmed his citizenship.Following his arrest, the suspect was transferred to the United Arab Emirates. A senior Israeli official told CBS News that UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan personally informed Netanyahu that he expected Saudi authorities to transfer the co-pilot to the UAE.Israeli investigators have since been sent to the UAE to join the locally led investigation and help determine whether the attack was orchestrated by outside parties.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Thursday described the Omani co-pilot accused of attacking Flydubai Captain Smit Machchhar as “suicidal” and said he had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination”. articles.title: Nepal avalanche kills at least 15 expedition workers
articles.summary: Rescuers recovered eight more bodies on Thursday from the area of an avalanche that swept through a mountain camp.
articles.body:
A Himalayan avalanche killed at least 15 expedition workers, as rescuers continued efforts to recover bodies from a mountain camp in central Nepal.

Rescuers recovered eight more bodies on Thursday from the area of the avalanche that swept through the base camp of the 7,126-metre (23,345-foot) Himlung peak early on Sunday, in one of the worst mountain disasters in recent years.

Nepali workers were pitching tents and ‌‌fixing ropes for later expeditions on the mountain located near the Chinese border.

Rescuers have so far recovered 15 bodies from the site, said Tul Singh Gurung, president of Nepal National Mountain Guide Association.

“The bodies that were recovered today ⁠⁠are expected to be brought by a helicopter to Kathmandu,” Gurung told Reuters.

He said chances of finding the one missing worker ⁠⁠were slim and the rescue operation is likely to wind up. The foreign climbers ⁠⁠had not reached the site ⁠⁠at the time of the avalanche.

A team of eleven rescuers, including experienced guides, were at the site, digging through more than four metres (14 feet) of snow which had buried tents at the base camp.

The bodies of two mountain guides were recovered on Sunday, and those of two kitchen staff were pulled out on Monday, followed by another three bodies on Tuesday.

Nepal’s worst mountaineering disasters in recent years occurred in 2014, when an avalanche killed 16 people on Everest, and in 2015, when an earthquake killed 18 people, also on Everest.

Authorities are still searching for bodies from devastating floods sparked by a mountain glacial collapse on 26 August that killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000 missing.

Heavy rain since Thursday has triggered more floods and landslides, killing at least 21 people, according to the national disaster agency.

Home to eight of the world’s 14 highest peaks, Nepal’s economy relies heavily on mountaineering and trekking tourism.

Himlung, where Sunday’s avalanche occurred, is a popular destination for mountaineers looking to begin climbing 7,000-metre peaks.

articles.title: Channel Islands' Christmas Lottery tickets go on sale
articles.summary: The Channel Islands' lottery, which raises money for charity, has a guaranteed top prize of £300k.
articles.body:
Tickets for the Channel Islands Christmas Lottery have gone on sale with a "guaranteed top prize of £300,000 that will increase as sales grow", organisers have said.

Jointly run by the States of Guernsey and Government of Jersey, the lottery has returned for its 51st year with the main draw set to take place in Guernsey on 17 December.

Organisers said the lottery had raised "tens of millions" for charities in the islands since it started in 1975.

The winning ticket in 2025 went to a Jersey ticket holder for the second year in a row, even though ticket sales were higher in Guernsey .

Head of lottery Jon Taylor said every pound raised after prizes and costs "continues to support worthy causes across our communities".

"We are proud that the lottery continues to contribute so much to charity and good causes that benefit the islands," he said.

Last year's jackpot was £493,320 but it was £1.1m a decade ago.

Taylor previously said falling jackpot sizes did not mean people had stopped playing, but instead reflected changing spending habits and increased competition for people's money.

He said sales had since improved with the introduction of a dedicated syndicate delivery service and keeping tickets at £2.

"Our primary objective is to maximise funding for good causes, but we are equally committed to keeping the lottery affordable and creating as many winners as possible from the available prize fund," he said.
